{
  "analysis": "The training data reveals that German legal texts frequently reference specific tax and judicial bodies (Finanzamt, Bundesfinanzgericht, Verwaltungsgerichtshof) often in genitive case (Finanzamtes, Bundesfinanzgerichtes) or as abbreviations (BFG). The rules must handle these variations and specific compound names (Magistrat der Stadt Wien) while avoiding false positives on common nouns.",
  "strategy": "Use specific regex patterns for known German legal entities, handling case variations (nominative/genitive) and abbreviations, with a priority order to match longer specific names before shorter generic ones.",
  "note": "Every rule includes output_template and output_key. Patterns use word boundaries to prevent partial matches.",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "match_finanzamt_variants",
      "description": "Matches 'Finanzamt' in various forms including genitive 'Finanzamtes' and specific regional names like 'Finanzamt Vorarlberg' or 'Finanzamt Österreich'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Finanzamt(?:es)?(?:\\s+(?:Vorarlberg|Österreich|Braunau\\s+Ried|Graz-Stadt))?|Finanzamtes\\s+(?:Braunau\\s+Ried|Österreich))\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "Covers the most frequent entity 'Finanzamt' and its specific regional variants found in the training data, handling both nominative and genitive cases."
    },
    {
      "name": "match_bundesfinanzgericht_variants",
      "description": "Matches 'Bundesfinanzgericht' and its genitive form 'Bundesfinanzgerichtes', plus the abbreviation 'BFG'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Bundesfinanzgericht(?:es)?|BFG)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 9,
      "reasoning": "Targets the primary appellate court entity and its common abbreviation, ensuring both full names and short forms are captured."
    },
    {
      "name": "match_verwaltungsgerichtshof_variants",
      "description": "Matches 'Verwaltungsgerichtshof' and its genitive form 'Verwaltungsgerichtshofes'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Verwaltungsgerichtshof(?:es)?)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 9,
      "reasoning": "Captures the Federal Administrative Court entity in both nominative and genitive cases as seen in legal reasoning sections."
    },
    {
      "name": "match_magistrat_wien",
      "description": "Matches 'Magistrat der Stadt Wien' and its variations including department numbers.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Magistrat(?:s)?\\s+der\\s+Stadt\\s+Wien(?:,\\s+Magistratsabteilung\\s+\\d+)?)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "Specifically targets the Vienna municipal authority which appears frequently in parking fine cases, handling the full name and departmental extensions."
    },
    {
      "name": "match_eu_gh_and_bfh",
      "description": "Matches European Court of Justice (EuGH) and Federal Fiscal Court (BFH) abbreviations.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Europäische\\s+Gerichtshof|EuGH|BFH)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "Captures higher court references often cited in legal arguments, ensuring abbreviations are recognized as organizations."
    },
    {
      "name": "match_law_firms_and_gmbh",
      "description": "Matches law firms and GmbH entities that appear as representatives or parties.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b([A-Z][a-zA-Z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-zA-Z]+)*\\s+(?:GmbH|GmbH\\s+&\\s+Partner\\s+KG|Stb\\s+OG|Wirtschaftstreuhand-?gesellschaft\\s+m\\.b\\.H))\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 5,
      "reasoning": "General pattern for commercial entities (law firms, GmbHs) which are organizations but distinct from government bodies, using structural cues like company suffixes."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": []
}

- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

IMPORTANT:
- Do NOT assume entities are capitalized; check the training data.
- Prefer structural patterns (\d+, [A-Z][a-z]+) over memorized alternations.
- When multiple entity types share similar text, use surrounding context to disambiguate.
